module_title: The Nernst Equation, Conductance & Integrated Rate Laws (Intermediate)
introduction: This level introduces the non-standard concentration dependencies of cell EMF (Nernst Equation), maps out electrolytic solution conductivity parameters, and solves the exact time-concentration mathematics for zero and first-order chemical kinetic systems.

core_concepts.title: The Nernst Equation
core_concepts.description: Calculates the electrode potential or cell EMF under non-standard concentrations and temperatures. At $298 \text{ K}$, it simplifies to: $E_{\text{cell}} = E^\circ_{\text{cell}} - \frac{0.0591}{n} \log_{10} Q$, where $n$ is the number of moles of electrons transferred, and $Q$ is the reaction quotient (Products/Reactants raised to stoichiometric powers). At equilibrium, $E_{\text{cell}} = 0$, giving $\log_{10} K_c = \frac{n E^\circ_{\text{cell}}}{0.0591}$.

core_concepts.title: Electrolytic Conductance & Kohlrausch's Law
core_concepts.description:
1. Conductivity ($\kappa$, Kappa): The inverse of resistivity. 
2. Molar Conductivity ($\Lambda_m$): Conductance of a solution containing 1 mole of electrolyte: $\Lambda_m = \frac{\kappa \times 1000}{C}$, where $C$ is Molar ity.
Kohlrausch's Law states that at infinite dilution, the molar conductivity of an electrolyte is the sum of the individual limiting molar conductivities of its constituent anions and cations: $\Lambda_m^\infty = \nu_+ \lambda_+^∞ + \nu_- \lambda_-^∞$.

core_concepts.title: Integrated Rate Law: Zero-Order Reactions
core_concepts.description: Reactions where the rate is entirely independent of reactant concentration: $-\frac{d[A]}{dt} = k$. Integration yields: $[A]_t = -kt + [A]_0$. The half-life is directly proportional to initial concentration: $t_{1/2} = \frac{[A]_0}{2k}$. The reaction goes to 100% completion in time $t_{\text{completion}} = [A]_0/k$.

core_concepts.title: Integrated Rate Law: First-Order Reactions
core_concepts.description: Reactions where the rate is directly proportional to concentration: $-\frac{d[A]}{dt} = k[A]$. Integration yields: $k = \frac{2.303}{t} \log_{10} \frac{[A]_0}{[A]_t}$. The half-life is completely independent of initial concentration: $t_{1/2} = \frac{\ln 2}{k} = \frac{0.693}{k}$. Most radioactive decays follow first-order kinetics.

important_entities.name: The Faraday Constant ($F$)
important_entities.significance: It represents the absolute electrical charge carried by exactly 1 mole of electrons ($6.022 \times 10^{23} \times 1.602 \times 10^{-19} \text{ C}$). Crucial for linking thermodynamic work with electrical transformations via $\Delta G = -nFE$.

trap_alerts_and_exceptions.alert_title: Conductivity vs. Molar Conductivity Dilution Trap
trap_alerts_and_exceptions.explanation: A high-frequency conceptual question: When a solution is diluted, the total number of ions per unit volume decreases. Therefore, specific Conductivity ($\kappa$) ALWAYS decreases upon dilution for both strong and weak electrolytes. However, Molar Conductivity ($\Lambda_m$) ALWAYS increases upon dilution because the volume containing 1 mole of electrolyte increases drastically, overriding the ion count drop.

mnemonics_and_tricks.memory_phrase: Two half-lives is 75%, Three is 87.5%, Ten is 99.9%
mnemonics_and_tricks.explanation:
Since first-order kinetics decay exponentially, memorize these milestones for rapid exam filtering: 
$t_{75\%} = 2 \times t_{1/2}$ 
$t_{87.5\%} = 3 \times t_{1/2}$ 
$t_{99.9\%} \approx 10 \times t_{1/2}$.

exam_strategy_tips: In Nernst Equation numerical problems, if a gas is involved at the electrode (e.g., $H_2$ gas at $2 \text{ atm}$), you must include its partial pressure in the reaction quotient ($Q$) expression exactly like a concentration term, raised to its stoichiometric power.
